en.sf.editorial.guide.title: Your first steps into written music
en.sf.editorial.guide.intro: You do not have to understand every symbol before making a start. Reading music is a collection of smaller skills: locating pitches, following durations, keeping a pulse, and noticing expression. Learn one layer, try it, then connect it to the next. This guide begins with the staff and ends with a practical routine you can repeat. A virtual keyboard is enough for the early examples. When you sit at a physical instrument, bring the same patient approach and choose a short passage with only a few new ideas.
en.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.title: What is sheet music?
en.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p0: Sheet music is a written way to communicate musical sounds and their timing. In standard staff notation, symbols show pitches, durations, silences, and expressive instructions. Read most music from left to right; notes aligned vertically often happen together. A score can contain a single melody or several parts that coordinate different performers. You do not need to hear a recording first to begin interpreting it, although listening can help you connect the symbols with the result. Think of the page as a set of relationships to understand, rather than a picture of finger movements that you must copy exactly.
en.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p1: Reading offers three practical benefits. First, it lets you approach music you have not memorized or heard repeatedly. Second, it helps you communicate: you can point to a measure, a note, or a rhythm when practicing with someone else. Third, it makes musical patterns visible. You can see where a melody repeats, where a chord changes, and how a phrase is organized. None of this makes playing by ear less valuable. Reading, listening, improvising, and remembering reinforce one another, so there is no need to choose one permanent learning identity before you start making music.
en.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p2: Before playing a page, take a brief survey. Find the clef at the beginning of each staff, the key signature if one appears, and the time signature. Look for the first note and any repeat signs. If there are two joined staves, notice which events line up. In this guide, you will first learn where notes live, then how their shapes organize time, and finally how rests and dynamics shape expression. Use the contents links to revisit one idea, and try the small examples before moving on. Accurate, comfortable reading begins with understanding a manageable amount of information.
en.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.title: The staff and clefs
en.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p0: A staff has five horizontal lines and four spaces. Count both from the bottom upward. A notehead can sit on a line, with the line passing through its center, or in a space between two lines. Moving to the next line or space moves one letter through the musical alphabet. The clef tells you which pitches those positions represent. Without checking it, a beautifully counted staff position may still produce the wrong answer. Start with the notehead rather than its stem: stem direction helps the notation fit together visually, but does not independently change a note's pitch.
en.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p1: Treble clef identifies G4 on the second line from the bottom. Its five lines are E4, G4, B4, D5, and F5. Remember E–G–B–D–F with Every Good Boy Does Fine, or another sentence you like. Its spaces spell FACE: F4, A4, C5, and E5. A mnemonic can get you started, but practice finding notes directly as well. For example, locate G4 using the clef, then move one position upward to A4 and one downward to F4. These nearby relationships will later help you read melodies more smoothly than reciting a sentence for every pitch.
en.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p2: Bass clef identifies F3 on the second line from the top, between the symbol's two dots. From bottom to top its lines are G2, B2, D3, F3, and A3; its spaces are A2, C3, E3, and G3. Good Boys Do Fine Always and All Cows Eat Grass are common memory aids. Notice that bass clef is not treble clef played vaguely lower: each written position has a specific meaning. Practice F3 and its neighbors until you can locate them without converting from a treble-clef answer in your head. Treat bass reading as its own useful skill.
en.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p3: Ledger lines are short extensions used for notes outside the staff. Middle C, C4, sits on the first ledger line below treble clef and the first ledger line above bass clef. Both symbols mean the same key. In the explorer, switch clefs while keeping the pitch fixed and watch its written position change. The sound stays the same because a clef changes the map, not the pitch you selected. Try D4 next: it sits in the space below the treble staff and above the middle-C ledger line in bass clef. Count every line and space, including those outside the staff.
en.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.title: Note names and the musical alphabet
en.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p0: Music uses seven letter names, A through G, which repeat in ascending order. Starting on C gives C, D, E, F, G, A, B, then another C. The distance between these two Cs is an octave. Scientific pitch notation adds a number so you can distinguish registers: middle C is C4, and the C an octave above is C5. The number changes at C, so B3 is immediately below C4. This labeling is especially useful on a virtual keyboard, where you may see only part of the instrument and cannot rely on a full piano's physical center to orient yourself.
en.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p1: On the keyboard, locate the repeating groups of two and three black keys. C is just to the left of a two-black-key group; F is just to the left of a three-black-key group. Move right along the white keys from C and say the alphabet aloud. Then move back left, reversing the names. Do not skip from G straight to a new C: A and B come between them. On the staff, the same sequence climbs through alternating lines and spaces. Select neighboring keys in the explorer and watch that movement, then try predicting the next written position before you press it.
en.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p2: A sharp raises a written note by one semitone, a flat lowers it by one semitone, and a natural cancels a prior alteration where applicable. On a piano, a semitone is the distance to the next key, black or white. E–F and B–C are semitones even though both keys are white. C-sharp and D-flat share a key in standard equal temperament, but the spelling depends on musical context. A key signature applies its listed sharps or flats throughout the music until changed; a local accidental normally applies to the same written pitch through the remainder of its measure. Begin with natural notes, then add these symbols deliberately.
en.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.title: Note values and rhythm
en.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p0: Pitch answers which note; rhythm answers when and for how long. A note's shape gives its duration relative to other notes. A whole note equals two half notes, four quarter notes, eight eighth notes, or sixteen sixteenth notes. These are ratios, not fixed seconds. In a passage where the quarter note receives one beat, a half note lasts two beats and a whole note lasts four. The tempo decides how quickly those beats pass. At a quarter-note tempo of 60 beats per minute, each quarter-note beat lasts one second; at 120, it lasts half a second.
en.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p1: Notice the visual differences. A whole note has an open notehead without a stem. A half note adds a stem; a quarter note fills the head. Eighth notes add one flag, and sixteenth notes add two. When grouped, beams replace the flags without changing the durations. Keep a steady pulse while saying one-and, two-and to divide each quarter-note beat into two eighth notes. For sixteenth notes, one-e-and-a divides it into four. The syllables are a counting aid; the important part is spacing each subdivision evenly instead of rushing the smaller notes.
en.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p2: A dot adds half of the original note value. A dotted half note equals three quarter notes; a dotted quarter equals three eighth notes. A tie joins notes of the same pitch into one continuous sound with their durations added. For example, a quarter tied to an eighth lasts one and a half quarter-note beats. Play the first note and continue holding through the second symbol without striking it again. A slur may look similar but generally groups different pitches into a phrase or articulation. Check whether the curved line connects identical pitches before interpreting it as a tie.
en.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p3: Try a rhythm before adding pitch. In 4/4, clap a half note followed by two quarter notes: clap on beat one, keep holding through beat two, then clap on three and four. Next replace the final quarter with two eighth notes, clapping four-and. Count aloud through the held notes instead of going silent mentally. If the pulse becomes uneven, slow down and repeat one measure. Then play the same rhythm on a single piano key. Adding a melody is a later step; a rhythm that feels clear on one note is much easier to keep steady while reading several pitches.
en.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.title: Time signatures and measures
en.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p0: Barlines divide music into measures, also called bars. The time signature near the beginning describes how durations are grouped. In simple meters such as 4/4 and 3/4, the top number gives the number of beats in a measure, and the bottom number identifies the note value for a beat. Four on the bottom means a quarter note. Count 4/4 as one, two, three, four, and 3/4 as one, two, three. Restart the count after the barline while keeping time continuous. A barline organizes the music; it does not automatically tell you to pause or lift your hands.
en.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p1: Compound meter needs a different reading. A typical 6/8 measure contains six eighth-note units organized into two groups of three. The main pulse is usually two dotted-quarter beats, each dividing into three eighth notes. Count ONE-two-three FOUR-five-six to feel the groups, or use two larger pulses with three subdivisions each. Do not assume 6/8 is simply six equally strong beats. It has the same total eighth-note duration as 3/4, but the usual grouping differs: 6/8 is three plus three, while 3/4 is two plus two plus two. Listen for how the accents organize that shared total.
en.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p2: Check a measure by adding its durations, including rests. In 4/4, two quarter notes plus one half note fill the bar. In 3/4, a dotted half note fills it. In 6/8, two dotted quarters do the same. A piece may begin with an incomplete pickup measure, so a short opening is not necessarily a printing mistake. Read the meter, look for repeated rhythmic groups, and count one complete measure before starting. When practicing with a metronome, decide which written note value the click represents; a number such as 80 is incomplete musical information without that beat-unit decision.
en.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.title: Rests and dynamics
en.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p0: A rest is a measured silence. It has a duration just like a sounding note, so you continue counting while not playing. Whole, half, quarter, eighth, and sixteenth rests correspond to those note values. A whole rest hangs below a staff line, while a half rest sits on a line. A whole-rest symbol may also indicate an entire measure of silence regardless of that measure's meter. Watch the context instead of assuming every whole-rest symbol always means exactly four quarter-note beats.
en.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p1: For a simple exercise, alternate a quarter note and a quarter rest in 4/4. Play on one, stay silent on two, play on three, and stay silent on four. Keep your counting continuous and release the note when the rest begins. On a real piano, a held sustain pedal can blur the silence, so practice without it at first. A rest is an active part of the phrase: it can separate ideas, create anticipation, or leave room for another instrument.
en.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p2: Dynamics describe relative loudness. Piano, written p, means soft; forte, f, means loud. Mezzo-piano and mezzo-forte, mp and mf, indicate moderately soft and moderately loud. These are musical relationships, not fixed volume measurements. A crescendo asks for increasing loudness and a diminuendo for decreasing loudness. On a physical keyboard, explore a comfortable range of touch without striking harshly. A basic virtual keyboard may play at a fixed level, so use the markings as reading practice even when the tool cannot reproduce every expressive nuance.
en.sf.editorial.guide.practice.title: A ten-minute reading routine
en.sf.editorial.guide.practice.p0: Spend the first two minutes locating a few anchor notes without guessing: middle C, treble G4, and bass F3. Say each name and find its key. Use minutes three and four for a small note drill in one clef, keeping the range narrow enough that you can explain your answers. If you miss a pitch, identify whether the error came from the clef, staff position, or octave. Write down one troublesome pair to revisit tomorrow. This makes your routine responsive to what you actually need rather than a fixed race to answer more questions.
en.sf.editorial.guide.practice.p1: During minutes five and six, clap a short rhythm and count aloud. During minutes seven and eight, combine that rhythm with a tiny melody. C–D–E–D–C is enough; you can also use a simple public-domain tune such as Hot Cross Buns or a beginner arrangement of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. Choose an arrangement whose range and rhythm match your current skill, because different versions can have very different difficulty. Read one measure ahead when possible, but stay slow enough to keep the pulse. If you lose your place, pause deliberately and restart from a clear point.
en.sf.editorial.guide.practice.p2: Use the final two minutes to play the short phrase again and notice one improvement and one next step. Perhaps the note names were faster but the rests still felt uncertain. Tomorrow, begin with that uncertainty. Short, regular sessions provide repeated chances to recall what you learned; long sessions are not a substitute for attention. When you are ready for a structured sequence, explore the piano lessons and continue using the free tools for focused review. Progress varies with experience and practice, so measure it by increasingly comfortable tasks rather than promising yourself a particular completion date.
en.sf.editorial.guide.faq.title: Common questions and your next step
en.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p0: How long does it take to read music? You can begin recognizing a few positions in a first session, but fluent reading develops through repeated practice with actual phrases. The timeline depends on the instrument, the music, and your prior experience. Aim first to read a small range accurately at a comfortable pace.
en.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p1: Do I need a teacher? You can learn basic symbols and practice recognition independently. A teacher can help with technique, listening, and habits that are hard to assess alone. These tools support practice, while your goals and the difficulties you encounter determine whether additional guidance would be useful.
en.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p2: Do I need a piano? A virtual keyboard is enough to connect early note names with sounds and staff positions. Learning to play an actual piano also requires touch, coordination, and comfortable movement, which an onscreen keyboard cannot fully teach. You can start reading before buying an instrument.
en.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p3: What should I do next? Return to the music notes trainer and try a small set without hints. Choose the treble or bass page for a focused review, or explore chords once single notes feel familiar. Keep this guide nearby and revisit the section that answers your next specific question.
en.sf.editorial.guide.explorer: Try it: keep a note, change the clef
en.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm-tip: Clap: half note → quarter note → two eighth notes. Count: ONE (hold two) THREE FOUR-and. The entire pattern fills one measure of 4/4.

en.sf.editorial.home.title: Music notes, from a first look to a familiar language
en.sf.editorial.home.intro: Read the position. Find the key. Hear the connection. These small steps turn the symbols on a page into something you can actually play.
en.sf.editorial.home.start.title: What a music note tells you
en.sf.editorial.home.start.p0: A written music note combines two useful instructions: which pitch to play and how long to hold it. Its position on the staff tells you the pitch, once you know the clef. Its shape tells you a relative duration. Begin by separating those jobs. You can learn to recognize a note without also solving a complicated rhythm at the same time.
en.sf.editorial.home.start.p1: In the trainer, look at the center of the notehead. Is a staff line running through it, or is it sitting in a space? That distinction matters more than the direction of the stem. A stem pointing up and a stem pointing down can represent the same pitch. Read the notehead first, then use the keyboard to connect that position with a sound.
en.sf.editorial.home.start.p2: A label such as C4 includes both a letter and an octave number. The letter identifies the note family; the number distinguishes this C from the many other Cs on a piano. C4 means middle C in scientific pitch notation. For a beginner, noticing the octave prevents a common mistake: choosing a correctly named key in the wrong register and wondering why the result sounds different.
en.sf.editorial.home.map.title: Find your way around the keyboard
en.sf.editorial.home.map.p0: The musical alphabet runs A, B, C, D, E, F, G, then begins again. On the piano, moving right usually means moving higher in pitch; moving left means lower. The white keys repeat the same seven letters. You do not need to memorize the entire keyboard at once. Learn one group, then notice that the pattern repeats across the instrument.
en.sf.editorial.home.map.p1: Use the black keys as landmarks. They appear in alternating groups of two and three. C is the white key immediately to the left of a group of two black keys. F is immediately to the left of a group of three. Once you locate C, walk along the white keys to find D, E, F, G, A, and B before reaching the next C.
en.sf.editorial.home.map.p2: Black keys belong to the same pitch system. The key between C and D can be called C-sharp or D-flat, depending on the notation and musical context. Start with the white keys if you are learning staff positions, then add sharps and flats. There is no black key between E and F or between B and C; these neighboring white keys are already a semitone apart.
en.sf.editorial.home.recognize.title: Read from landmarks, then recognize patterns
en.sf.editorial.home.recognize.p0: A clef fixes the meaning of the staff. In treble clef, the second line from the bottom is G4. In bass clef, the second line from the top is F3. These are useful anchor notes. Identify the clef before guessing a letter: the same visual position on two different clefs does not normally mean the same pitch. One quick check can prevent an entire chain of mistakes.
en.sf.editorial.home.recognize.p1: From a known note, move one letter for every neighboring line or space. A step from a line to the next space moves to the next letter. A move from one line to the next line skips a letter and forms a third. Practice seeing those distances. Counting from the bottom of the staff every time works, but eventually slows you down when a melody has many notes.
en.sf.editorial.home.recognize.p2: Combine memory and movement. First recognize a landmark such as middle C, treble G, or bass F. Then describe the next note as one step above or a third below. When the same position comes back several times, try naming it directly. This approach helps you read both an isolated note in a quiz and a sequence in real music, where neighboring notes provide valuable clues.
en.sf.editorial.home.connect.title: Use the trainer and explorer for different jobs
en.sf.editorial.home.connect.p0: In a note drill, commit to an answer before revealing it. Look at the clef, name the letter and octave, then choose the matching key. Immediate feedback is useful because you can compare your reasoning with the correct position while the question is still fresh. If you miss a note, find one nearby landmark and explain the distance to yourself before continuing.
en.sf.editorial.home.connect.p1: The keyboard explorer reverses that process: select a key and inspect where its note appears on the staff. Use it when a position feels unfamiliar, or compare the same pitch under different clefs. This is exploration rather than a scored test. Play adjacent white keys slowly and watch the notehead alternate between lines and spaces; the movement makes the abstract alphabet much easier to understand.
en.sf.editorial.home.connect.p2: Sound adds another connection, but it does not replace reading. Listen to the selected key after you have identified its notation. Ask whether the pitch moved up, down, or stayed the same. Keep the volume comfortable and take your time. A virtual keyboard is enough for this recognition exercise, although a physical piano will eventually add finger movement, touch, and coordination to the task.
en.sf.editorial.home.practice.title: Make a short session count
en.sf.editorial.home.practice.p0: Choose one small goal for each session, such as recognizing the five treble lines or finding every C in the displayed range. Spend a minute exploring those positions, then answer a short set without help. Read the result as information about what to revisit. A high score on familiar notes is encouraging, but a lower score on a new clef can still represent useful learning.
en.sf.editorial.home.practice.p1: After a mistake, avoid immediately pressing random keys until the feedback turns positive. Say the correct note, locate it again, and compare it with your original answer. Were you one staff position away, using the wrong clef, or an octave too high? Naming the type of error gives your next attempt a purpose and makes practice more productive than simply repeating the same number of questions.
en.sf.editorial.home.practice.p2: Finish by reading a tiny pattern away from the quiz: C–D–E–D–C, for example. Name the notes, find them on the keyboard, and play them with an even pulse. When letter names feel comfortable, move to the dedicated treble or bass trainer for a wider range. The reading guide introduces note lengths and meter so that these separate pitches can begin to sound like a phrase.
en.sf.editorial.treble.title: Make the treble staff feel familiar
en.sf.editorial.treble.intro: Learn the reference points first, then read the spaces between them. A few dependable landmarks are more useful than a hurried guess.
en.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.title: Begin with the G-clef landmark
en.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p0: Treble clef is also called the G clef. Its curl centers on the second staff line from the bottom, identifying that line as G4. From there, the other lines and spaces follow the musical alphabet. Check this landmark whenever you begin a new exercise. The clef is part of the instruction, not a decorative symbol you can ignore once the notes appear.
en.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p1: The treble staff commonly represents music in a higher register, including much right-hand piano writing. It is also used by many other instruments and voices. It does not mean that every note must be played with the right hand. A piano score can change clefs when the range changes, and fingering or hand distribution is a separate decision from identifying the written pitch.
en.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p2: Build three starting points: middle C on its short ledger line below the staff, G4 on the second line, and C5 in the third space. Find each on the keyboard, then return to the staff. These anchors divide the range into smaller neighborhoods. Instead of counting a long distance from the bottom, you can start with whichever known note lies closest to the question.
en.sf.editorial.treble.lines.title: Learn lines and spaces in order
en.sf.editorial.treble.lines.p0: Read treble lines from bottom to top as E4, G4, B4, D5, and F5. The familiar phrase Every Good Boy Does Fine can help recall E–G–B–D–F. Use any sentence that you remember easily, but keep its direction clear. Starting at the top reverses the sequence. A mnemonic is a temporary memory aid, not a rule about how melodies must move.
en.sf.editorial.treble.lines.p1: The four spaces, also read from bottom to top, spell F4, A4, C5, and E5: FACE. Notice that the lines and spaces interleave. Beginning on the bottom line, the complete sequence is E4, F4, G4, A4, B4, C5, D5, E5, F5. Practice that combined sequence so that you do not treat line notes and space notes as two unrelated systems.
en.sf.editorial.treble.lines.p2: Look at the notehead rather than the stem or flag. A note on the middle line is B4 whether its stem points upward or downward. If the notehead is centered between two lines, it belongs to that space even when its stem crosses several others. Slowing down to locate the notehead accurately is usually more helpful than repeating a mnemonic faster under pressure.
en.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.title: Read beyond the five lines
en.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p0: Ledger lines extend the staff when a pitch is too low or high to fit comfortably inside it. Middle C, or C4, sits on the first ledger line below the treble staff. D4 occupies the space between that ledger line and the bottom staff line. E4 is on the bottom line itself. Learn this three-note doorway as one connected pattern rather than three separate facts.
en.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p1: Above the staff, G5 sits in the space immediately above the top line, and A5 is on the first ledger line above it. The alphabet continues without a new rule. Each move to the next line or space advances one letter. Count the spaces as well as the short lines; counting only ledger lines makes it easy to skip a note and answer a third too high.
en.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p2: Octave numbers help distinguish repeated letters across this range. C4 and C5 are both C, but they are different keys and different sounds. The number changes when B moves up to C, so B4 is followed by C5. If the trainer expects a specific pitch, check both parts of the name. A correct letter in the wrong octave is a useful clue about a register-reading mistake.
en.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.title: Turn single notes into melodic shapes
en.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p0: Once you can find individual pitches, begin reading how they relate. E4–F4–G4 moves upward by steps, alternating line, space, line. E4–G4–B4 moves upward by thirds, staying on lines. You can often see those patterns before naming every note. Find the first pitch carefully, then follow the shape while checking the names. This makes the staff feel like a map of movement.
en.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p1: Repeated notes deserve attention too. Several identical noteheads in a row keep the same pitch even if their rhythms differ. A melody can also return to a familiar position after a leap. Scan a short phrase for repetitions before playing it. Grouping repeated material reduces the number of new decisions you need to make and leaves more attention available for rhythm and a steady pulse.
en.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p2: Sharps, flats, and naturals modify a written pitch without moving its letter position on the staff. F-sharp is still written on an F line or space, with an accidental or key signature supplying the alteration. When you begin working with accidentals, identify the letter first and then apply the symbol. This two-step method prevents confusing a black piano key with an entirely new staff position.
en.sf.editorial.treble.practice.title: A focused treble-clef routine
en.sf.editorial.treble.practice.p0: Start a session by locating G4, C5, and middle C without a hint. Then practice a small group around one landmark, such as E4 through A4. Expand the range only when those positions feel dependable. Mixing every possible pitch immediately can make it difficult to tell whether the problem is a single unfamiliar note, ledger-line counting, or simply too many new positions at once.
en.sf.editorial.treble.practice.p1: Use the answer reveal as a teaching step after making a real attempt. Compare the correct position with the one you expected, then say the note name before choosing the next question. Keep track of the notes you confuse, especially neighboring line and space positions. On the next session, explore those pairs on the keyboard before testing them again. Deliberate correction matters more than protecting a streak.
en.sf.editorial.treble.practice.p2: Finally, read a five-note melody at a comfortable speed, keeping the pulse even enough to continue through a small hesitation. You might use C4–D4–E4–D4–C4 with one equal-length note per pulse. When this becomes easy, change the rhythm or starting note, but not both at once. Explore bass clef next to understand how the other half of a piano score connects to the same keyboard.
en.sf.editorial.bass.title: Read bass notes with a clear sense of direction
en.sf.editorial.bass.intro: The lower staff follows the same alphabet. New landmarks help you read it on its own terms and connect it to the whole piano.
en.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.title: What the bass clef actually changes
en.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p0: Bass clef assigns a different set of pitches to the staff than treble clef does. Its two dots sit on either side of the second line from the top, marking that line as F3. That is why it is also called the F clef. Begin every bass exercise by noticing those dots. Reading a bass note with a memorized treble pattern produces the wrong pitch.
en.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p1: The bass staff is useful for lower music: bass voices, instruments such as cello and bassoon, and many left-hand piano parts. Lower register does not mean simpler music. A bass line can carry a melody, establish a chord, or create a rhythmic pattern. Learning to read it independently gives you access to musical information that is easy to miss when you focus only on a tune above it.
en.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p2: On a piano, the staff does not permanently belong to a particular hand. The left hand often plays bass-clef material, but clefs describe pitch ranges, not fingers. Keep these ideas separate while practicing. First identify the written pitch and locate its key. Later, use the score, fingering, and musical context to decide which hand should play it and how to move comfortably between notes.
en.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.title: Use F3, the spaces, and the lines
en.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p0: Bass-clef lines from bottom to top are G2, B2, D3, F3, and A3. A common memory phrase is Good Boys Do Fine Always. The four spaces are A2, C3, E3, and G3, often remembered as All Cows Eat Grass. Say the letters as well as the sentence. The goal is to recognize G2 or C3 directly, rather than mentally reciting a whole phrase for every note.
en.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p1: Use F3 as your central anchor because the clef itself points to it. One staff step below is E3 in a space; one step above is G3 in a space. D3 lies on the middle line. Those neighboring pitches give you a compact region to practice first. Play D3–E3–F3–G3 slowly while watching the noteheads alternate between lines and spaces on the display.
en.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p2: Another useful reference is C3 in the second space from the bottom. Compare it with middle C, C4, above the staff: the letters match but the octave differs. Finding both on a keyboard helps prevent treating every C as the same key. When a question feels difficult, identify a nearby landmark and count individual lines and spaces outward instead of restarting from the lowest staff line.
en.sf.editorial.bass.register.title: Connect ledger lines and middle C
en.sf.editorial.bass.register.p0: Middle C is written on the first ledger line above the bass staff. Immediately below it, B3 sits in the space above the top line, and A3 sits on that top line. This A3–B3–C4 sequence is a useful bridge toward treble clef. Middle C below a treble staff and middle C above a bass staff represent exactly the same piano key, not two neighboring Cs.
en.sf.editorial.bass.register.p1: Below the bass staff, F2 sits in the space beneath the bottom line and E2 lies on the first ledger line below it. Continue downward through the alphabet in reverse: E, D, C, B, A, G, F. Octave numbers decrease when you move down from C to B. For example, descending from C3 leads to B2, not B3. This is notation for register, not a change in the alphabet itself.
en.sf.editorial.bass.register.p2: The grand staff joins treble and bass staves with a brace in many piano scores. Think of it as two readable windows into one continuous pitch range. Notes written above bass and below treble can overlap, because the choice of clef also serves readability. Do not assume that the empty printed gap between the staves represents a special musical interval; spacing on the page can change.
en.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.title: See the shape of a bass line
en.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p0: Bass parts often become easier when you recognize intervals rather than isolated letters. A line-to-next-line movement is a third; a line-to-neighboring-space movement is a step. Try C3–E3–G3, the notes of a C major triad. All three occupy spaces in bass clef. Notice their visual shape, then compare it with D3–F3–A3 on lines. The distances look alike even though the notes differ.
en.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p1: An accompaniment may alternate a low root note with a chord, or move between a root and its fifth. Before playing, identify repeated pitches and recurring shapes. You still need to read accidentals and rhythm, but recognizing the pattern gives the passage some structure. Avoid assuming that every low note is the root of the current chord; inversions and moving bass lines can put other chord tones underneath.
en.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p2: Read vertically as well as horizontally when several noteheads are stacked. They normally sound together as a chord rather than as a fast sequence. Name the lowest pitch first, then inspect the intervals above it. If the span is unfamiliar, use the keyboard explorer to hear the notes separately before combining them. This keeps the reading task clear while you build the coordination needed to play them together.
en.sf.editorial.bass.practice.title: Build accuracy before adding hand movement
en.sf.editorial.bass.practice.p0: Practice bass clef by itself for part of your session, even if your treble reading is already comfortable. Begin with F3, D3, and C3, then add their neighbors. Naming a pitch aloud and selecting its key is enough at first. You do not need to play a difficult left-hand pattern while also learning the note positions. Separating these demands makes the source of a mistake easier to see.
en.sf.editorial.bass.practice.p1: When you miss an answer, check three things in order: the clef, the line or space, and the octave. If you repeatedly answer with a treble name, spend a minute returning to the F3 landmark. If the letter is right but the register is wrong, compare the two matching letter names on the keyboard. Use the result to choose the next practice target rather than simply restarting the score.
en.sf.editorial.bass.practice.p2: End with a small musical task, such as reading C3–G2–C3–E3 with equal note lengths. Keep the pulse slow and listen to the direction of each move. Later, combine one bass note with a simple treble melody to connect both staves. The piano chord finder can help you hear how a low note supports harmony, while the reading guide adds the rhythmic symbols needed for complete phrases.
en.sf.editorial.chords.title: Understand the notes behind every piano chord
en.sf.editorial.chords.intro: Choose a root, compare a chord quality, and listen closely. The useful part is discovering why a small change in notes creates a different sound.
en.sf.editorial.chords.formula.title: Build a chord from a root and a formula
en.sf.editorial.chords.formula.p0: A chord combines notes that are heard together, or understood together when played in sequence. A basic triad uses three different note names: a root, a third, and a fifth. The root gives the chord its name. In C major, C is the root, E is the third, and G is the fifth. These names describe relationships to C, not fixed locations on the keyboard.
en.sf.editorial.chords.formula.p1: The finder turns that relationship into visible keys. Select a root note, choose the chord type, then find the result. Read the note names before playing the sound. Comparing the keyboard highlights with the labels helps you understand the chord as a set of pitches rather than a hand shape to memorize. You can build the same quality from another root by preserving the distances between its notes.
en.sf.editorial.chords.formula.p2: Those distances can be measured in semitones, the smallest steps between neighboring piano keys. Count both black and white keys. From C to C-sharp is one semitone, and from E to F is also one. A major triad places notes at zero, four, and seven semitones above the root. Count movements rather than counting the starting key as one, otherwise every interval will be one step short.
en.sf.editorial.chords.quality.title: Hear what changes between chord types
en.sf.editorial.chords.quality.p0: A minor triad uses zero, three, and seven semitones above its root. Compare C major, C–E–G, with C minor, C–E-flat–G. Only the third changes, yet the color of the chord shifts. Major and minor are structural labels; they are not guarantees that a passage must sound happy or sad. Tempo, register, rhythm, and the surrounding harmony all influence how a listener experiences the result.
en.sf.editorial.chords.quality.p1: A dominant seventh chord adds a minor seventh to a major triad: C7 contains C, E, G, and B-flat. A major seventh chord uses B-natural instead, so Cmaj7 is C, E, G, B. These symbols are not interchangeable. Listen to them back to back with the same root and register. Concentrating on the changed upper note makes the distinction easier to hear than comparing two unrelated chords.
en.sf.editorial.chords.quality.p2: Suspended chords replace the third. Csus4 contains C, F, and G, while Csus2 contains C, D, and G. Without E or E-flat, neither is a standard major or minor triad. Diminished and augmented triads change the fifth as well: C diminished uses C, E-flat, G-flat, and C augmented uses C, E, G-sharp. Introduce these types one at a time and describe which key moved between examples.
en.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.title: Keep the chord, change the lowest note
en.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p0: An inversion rearranges a chord so a note other than the root becomes the lowest pitch. C–E–G is root-position C major. E–G–C is its first inversion, and G–C–E is its second inversion. The set of note names remains C, E, and G. Use the inversion control to compare these arrangements and listen to how a different bass note changes the weight of the same harmony.
en.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p1: A slash symbol can name the bass explicitly. C/E means a C major chord with E in the bass; it does not mean a C chord followed by an E chord. This is useful when reading a song chart because the bass line may move while the harmony stays closely related. Check the lowest highlighted key in the finder, then identify the remaining chord tones above it.
en.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p2: Finger numbers describe a suggested hand position, not the definition of a chord. Piano fingers are numbered one through five from thumb to little finger on either hand. A comfortable fingering depends on hand size, register, inversion, and the notes before and after the chord. Treat a displayed fingering as a starting point. Avoid forcing a stretch; you can practice the pitches separately while deciding on a comfortable movement.
en.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.title: Listen to chords as a sequence
en.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p0: A progression is an ordered series of chords. C–G–Am–F uses C major, G major, A minor, and F major. In the key of C major, these are commonly labeled I–V–vi–IV. The numerals describe scale-degree roots and chord quality, making it possible to recognize the same pattern in another key. Uppercase numerals here indicate major triads; the lowercase vi indicates a minor triad.
en.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p1: Compare that sequence with G–D–Em–C. It follows I–V–vi–IV in G major, so the relationships are similar although the pitches have moved. Play each progression at a steady pace, then sing or hum the bass roots if comfortable. Listen for the change from one chord to the next rather than trying to label each sound as an emotion. Context is part of what makes harmony interesting.
en.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p2: Inversions can make a progression easier to play by keeping neighboring chords close together. For example, C–E–G can move to B–D–G for a G chord with B in the bass. The top G stays in place while the other voices move downward. This is a simple example of voice leading. Explore nearby notes before assuming that every new chord must be played in root position with a large hand jump.
en.sf.editorial.chords.practice.title: Practice a useful comparison, not a long list
en.sf.editorial.chords.practice.p0: Choose one root and compare major, minor, and suspended fourth chords. Before listening, predict which note should change. Then check the highlights and say the complete set of note names. This turns the finder into an active exercise. If you only press play repeatedly, the sounds may become familiar without building the ability to construct a chord when you encounter its symbol on a new chart.
en.sf.editorial.chords.practice.p1: Next, build the same chord quality on a different root. Remember that black keys can have different written names depending on context. D-flat and C-sharp share a piano key in standard equal temperament, but correct chord spelling still follows the letter relationships of the formula. In a D major triad, the third is F-sharp, not G-flat, because D to F uses the letter distance of a third.
en.sf.editorial.chords.practice.p2: Finish with two or four chords and a slow pulse. Play each as a block, then as separate notes, keeping the total time for each chord consistent. If a change is awkward, practice just that transition before returning to the full sequence. The music notes trainers strengthen the staff-to-key connection, and the reading guide explains note values so you can turn chord symbols and highlighted keys into a timed musical part.

zh.sf.editorial.guide.title: 迈出读谱的第一步
zh.sf.editorial.guide.intro: 不必认识全部符号，才开始学习音乐。读谱由几个小能力组成：定位音高、理解时值、保持拍子、注意表情。学一层，试一试，再连接下一层。本指南从五线谱讲起，以可重复的练习计划结束。前面的例子用虚拟键盘就能完成。坐到实体乐器前，也请保持耐心，选择只包含少量新知识的短片段。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.title: 什么是乐谱？
zh.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p0: 乐谱用书写方式传达声音及其时间安排。标准五线谱的符号表示音高、时值、休止和表情。通常从左往右阅读，纵向对齐的音往往同时发生。乐谱可以只有一条旋律，也可以协调多个演奏者的声部。即使没有先听录音，也能开始理解它；聆听则帮助你把符号与声音联系起来。把页面看成需要理解的一组关系，而不是必须机械模仿的手指动作图。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p1: 识谱有三个实际好处。第一，你能接触没有背熟、甚至没听过的新音乐。第二，练习交流更准确：可以指出某个小节、音符或节奏。第三，音乐结构变得可见，你能看到旋律重复、和弦变化与乐句组织。这并不降低听觉学习的价值。读谱、聆听、即兴和记忆互相支持，无须在开始前把自己限定为某一种学习者。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.sheet-music.p2: 弹奏前先快速浏览：找每行开头的谱号、可能出现的调号与拍号，看看首音和反复记号。若有两行相连的谱表，注意哪些事件对齐。本指南先介绍音符位置，再讲形状如何组织时间，最后讲休止和力度。用目录返回需要复习的部分，做完小例子再继续。准确、舒适的读谱，始于理解适量信息。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.title: 五线谱与谱号
zh.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p0: 五线谱有五条横线、四个间，都从下往上数。符头可以在线上，线穿过其中心，也可以在两条线之间。移动到相邻的线或间，音乐字母表前进一步。谱号指定这些位置对应的音高，不检查谱号，位置数得再准确也可能答错。先看符头，不要看符干：符干方向有助于谱面排布，本身不会改变音高。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p1: 高音谱号指定从下往上第二线为 G4。五条线是 E4、G4、B4、D5、F5，可用 Every Good Boy Does Fine 记忆；四个间是 F4、A4、C5、E5，拼成 FACE。口诀能帮助入门，也要练直接认音。例如先由谱号找到 G4，再向上一格找到 A4，向下一格找到 F4。这些相邻关系比每个音都背口诀更适合流畅读旋律。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p2: 低音谱号的两点夹着从上往下第二线，指定为 F3。五条线从下往上是 G2、B2、D3、F3、A3，四个间是 A2、C3、E3、G3。英语口诀分别为 Good Boys Do Fine Always 和 All Cows Eat Grass。低音谱号不是把高音谱号模糊地弹低一些，每个位置有准确含义。练熟 F3 与邻音，不必先在脑中算高音答案，再换成低音。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.staff-clefs.p3: 加线是谱表外的短延伸线。中央 C（C4）在高音谱表下加一线、低音谱表上加一线，两者对应同一个键。在探索器中固定音高并切换谱号，观察位置变化。声音不变，因为谱号改变的是地图，不是所选音高。再试 D4：它在高音谱表下方的间，也在低音谱表中央 C 加线上方的间。数位置时，每条线和每个间都要计入。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.title: 音名与音乐字母表
zh.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p0: 音乐使用 A 到 G 七个循环字母。从 C 出发是 C、D、E、F、G、A、B，再到 C，两个 C 相距一个八度。科学音高记号加数字区分音区：中央 C 是 C4，高八度是 C5。编号在 C 处改变，所以 C4 紧下方是 B3。虚拟键盘往往只展示一部分音域，这些标签能帮助定位，不必依赖完整钢琴的物理中心。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p1: 键盘上黑键以两键组和三键组重复。C 在两黑键左侧，F 在三黑键左侧。从 C 沿白键向右念音名，再向左逆序念。G 后不是直接跳到 C，中间还有 A 与 B。谱表上，同一序列在线和间之间交替上行。在探索器中点相邻琴键观察移动，再试着先预测下一个位置，随后按键验证。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.alphabet.p2: 升号将音升高一个半音，降号降低一个半音，还原号在适用位置取消之前的变音。钢琴上半音是到下一个黑键或白键的距离，E–F、B–C 虽然都是白键，也只相差半音。标准十二平均律中升 C 与降 D 共用一键，拼写取决于语境。调号中的升降音持续适用，直到改变；临时变音记号通常作用于本小节剩余部分的同一记谱音高。先练本位音，再有意识地加入这些符号。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.title: 音符时值与节奏
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p0: 音高回答弹什么，节奏回答何时弹、持续多久。音符形状表示相对时值：一个全音符等于两个二分、四个四分、八个八分或十六个十六分音符。这些是比例，不是固定秒数。当四分音符为一拍，二分音符持续两拍，全音符四拍。速度决定每拍多快：以四分音符为拍、每分钟 60 拍时，一拍一秒；120 拍时，一拍半秒。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p1: 观察外形：全音符为空心符头、无符干；二分音符增加符干；四分音符填实符头。八分音符加一道符尾，十六分加两道。成组时用符杠替代符尾，时值不变。保持拍子，念 one-and、two-and，把每个四分拍均分成两个八分；念 one-e-and-a 则均分成四个十六分。音节只是辅助，关键是均匀分拍，不把短音越弹越快。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p2: 附点增加原时值的一半。附点二分等于三个四分，附点四分等于三个八分。延音线连接相同音高，把时值相加并持续发声。例如四分连八分，持续一个半四分拍：只弹第一个符号，不在第二个再次触键。圆滑线形状相似，但通常把不同音高连接成乐句或奏法。先检查弧线是否连接相同音高，再判断是否为延音线。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm.p3: 先练节奏，再加音高。4/4 中拍一个二分音符、两个四分：第一拍拍手，第二拍保持，第三和第四拍各拍一次。再把最后一个四分换成两个八分，念 four-and。长音期间也在心里或出声数拍。若拍子不稳，就减速只练一个小节，然后把同样节奏弹在单个琴键上。单音能保持稳定后，再加入旋律。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.title: 拍号与小节
zh.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p0: 小节线把音乐分成小节。开头附近的拍号说明时值如何分组。4/4、3/4 等单拍子中，上方数字表示每小节拍数，下方数字指定一拍的音符时值；下方为 4，表示四分音符。4/4 数一二三四，3/4 数一二三。跨小节线后重新计数，但时间连续。小节线负责组织音乐，不自动要求停顿或抬手。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p1: 复拍子要换一种读法。典型 6/8 小节有六个八分单位，通常分成两组三个。主要脉动通常是两个附点四分拍，每拍再分三个八分。可数“一二三、四五六”，重音落在一与四，或感觉两大拍各含三个细分。别把 6/8 简化成六个同样强的拍。它与 3/4 的八分总时长相同，但通常分组不同：6/8 是三加三，3/4 是二加二加二。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.time-signatures.p2: 检查小节时，把音符和休止符时值一起相加。4/4 中两个四分加一个二分填满小节；3/4 中一个附点二分填满；6/8 中两个附点四分填满。音乐也可能以不完整的弱起小节开始，开头不足一小节未必是印刷错误。开始前读拍号、看重复节奏组并数一个完整小节。使用节拍器时还需决定每次点击代表哪种音符，仅有“80”并不足以说明音乐速度。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.title: 休止符与力度
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p0: 休止符是有时值的安静，不弹时仍继续数拍。全、二分、四分、八分、十六分休止符对应相关音符时值。全休止符悬在线下，二分休止符坐在线上。全休止符号也可表示整小节休止，与小节拍号无关，所以要看上下文，不能认为它永远等于四个四分拍。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p1: 做一个简单练习：4/4 中交替四分音符与四分休止。第一拍弹、第二拍静、第三拍弹、第四拍静。保持连续计数，并在休止开始时放开琴键。实体钢琴上，延音踏板可能模糊休止，初练先不用踏板。休止是乐句的主动部分，可分隔想法、制造期待，或给其他乐器留下空间。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rests-dynamics.p2: 力度描述相对响度：p（piano）为弱，f（forte）为强，mp 与 mf 为中弱和中强。它们是音乐关系，不是固定音量测量。渐强要求逐渐变响，渐弱要求逐渐变轻。在实体钢琴上用舒适触键探索，避免粗暴敲击。基础虚拟键盘可能音量固定，无法表现所有细节，但仍可借此练习读懂力度记号。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.practice.title: 每天十分钟读谱计划
zh.sf.editorial.guide.practice.p0: 前两分钟不靠猜测找到几个参照音：中央 C、高音 G4、低音 F3，念音名并找琴键。第三、四分钟在一种谱号的小范围内答题，确保能解释自己的答案。出错时检查是谱号、位置还是八度问题，记下一对容易混淆的音，明天复习。让练习回应实际需求，而不是固定地追求答更多题。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.practice.p1: 第五、六分钟拍短节奏并出声数拍；第七、八分钟把它与小旋律结合，C–D–E–D–C 已经足够，也可用公版民歌 Hot Cross Buns 或 Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star 的初级改编。不同版本难度差异很大，选择匹配当前音域与节奏能力的版本。尽量提前看下一小节，但速度要慢到能保持拍子。找不到位置时，有意识地暂停，从清楚的起点重来。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.practice.p2: 最后两分钟重弹乐句，发现一个进步和一个下一步目标。例如音名更快了，但休止还不稳，明天就从休止开始。短而规律的练习提供反复回忆机会，长时间不能替代专注。准备好系统学习时可探索钢琴课程，继续用免费工具针对复习。进度因经验和练习而异，用越来越舒适的任务衡量进步，不给自己承诺固定完成日期。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.faq.title: 常见问题与下一步
zh.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p0: 学会读谱要多久？第一节就可以开始认识几个位置，但流畅阅读需要反复练真实乐句。时间取决于乐器、曲目和已有经验。先把目标设为：在小音域内，以舒适速度准确阅读。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p1: 需要老师吗？基础符号与认音可以自学。老师可以帮助处理自己难以观察的技巧、聆听和习惯问题。工具用于辅助练习，是否需要更多指导，取决于你的目标与实际遇到的困难。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p2: 必须有钢琴吗？虚拟键盘足以把初步音名、声音和谱表位置连起来。真正弹钢琴还需要触键、协调与舒适动作，屏幕键盘无法完整教授。买乐器之前，也能开始读谱。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.faq.p3: 下一步做什么？返回音符练习器，做一小组不看提示的题。选择高音或低音页面针对复习，单音熟悉后再探索和弦。把指南留在手边，遇到具体问题时返回对应章节。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.explorer: 试一试：保留音高，切换谱号
zh.sf.editorial.guide.rhythm-tip: 拍手：二分 → 四分 → 两个八分。数拍：第一拍拍手（第二拍保持），第三拍拍手，第四拍均分两下。整个节奏恰好填满一个 4/4 小节。
zh.sf.editorial.guide.source: 延伸阅读：Open Music Theory 的复拍子说明
zh.sf.editorial.kicker: 懂一点乐理，多一份音乐的乐趣
zh.sf.editorial.home.title: 从第一次看见音符，到读懂音乐的语言
zh.sf.editorial.home.intro: 看位置，找琴键，听声音。通过这些小步骤，把纸上的符号变成你能弹出的音乐。
zh.sf.editorial.home.start.title: 一个音符告诉你什么
zh.sf.editorial.home.start.p0: 书写的音符包含两类信息：弹哪个音，以及持续多久。确定谱号后，音符在五线谱上的位置告诉你音高，音符的形状表示相对时值。刚开始可以把这两件事分开学习，不必一边认音，一边处理复杂节奏。
zh.sf.editorial.home.start.p1: 练习时先看符头的中心：它在一条线上，还是在两条线之间？这比符干朝上还是朝下更重要。相同音高的符干可能有不同方向。先读符头的位置，再用键盘把这个位置和实际声音联系起来。
zh.sf.editorial.home.start.p2: C4 这样的标签由音名和八度编号组成。字母表示音名，数字把它与钢琴上的其他 C 区分开。在科学音高记号中，C4 就是中央 C。注意八度，可以避免一个常见错误：找对了音名字母，却弹到另一个音区。
zh.sf.editorial.home.map.title: 找到键盘上的方向
zh.sf.editorial.home.map.p0: 音乐字母表按 A、B、C、D、E、F、G 循环。钢琴上向右通常音高升高，向左降低。白键不断重复这七个音名。你不必一次记住整架钢琴，先认识一组，再观察相同图案如何重复。
zh.sf.editorial.home.map.p1: 黑键是很好的定位参照：它们以两个、三个为一组交替出现。两个黑键左边紧邻的白键是 C，三个黑键左边紧邻的白键是 F。找到 C 后，向右依次找到 D、E、F、G、A、B，再到下一个 C。
zh.sf.editorial.home.map.p2: 黑键也属于这套音高系统。C 和 D 之间的黑键可以记为升 C 或降 D，具体取决于乐谱和音乐语境。先用白键熟悉谱表位置，再学习升降号。E 与 F、B 与 C 之间没有黑键，因为这两对相邻白键本来就相差一个半音。
zh.sf.editorial.home.recognize.title: 先找参照音，再看音程形状
zh.sf.editorial.home.recognize.p0: 谱号决定各条线和间表示什么音。高音谱号从下往上第二线是 G4；低音谱号从上往下第二线是 F3。这两个音是实用的定位点。回答前先检查谱号，因为同一视觉位置在不同谱号中通常不是同一个音。
zh.sf.editorial.home.recognize.p1: 从已知音出发，每移动到相邻的线或间，音名就前进一步。从线到相邻间是级进；从一条线到下一条线，跳过一个字母，构成三度。练习辨认这些距离，比每次都从底线重新数更适合阅读连续旋律。
zh.sf.editorial.home.recognize.p2: 把记忆与移动方向结合起来：先找中央 C、高音 G 或低音 F，再判断下一个音在其上方一步，还是下方三度。相同位置出现多次后，尝试直接认出音名。这样既能回答单音题，也能借助相邻音的关系阅读真正的旋律。
zh.sf.editorial.home.connect.title: 让练习器和键盘探索器各司其职
zh.sf.editorial.home.connect.p0: 答题时先做出自己的判断，再查看答案。观察谱号，说出音名和八度，然后选择琴键。即时反馈让你趁记忆还清晰时核对思路。答错后，找一个附近的参照音，说明两者相距几步，再继续下一题。
zh.sf.editorial.home.connect.p1: 键盘探索器把过程倒过来：选择琴键，观察它在五线谱上的位置。不熟悉某个音，或想比较同一音高在两种谱号中的写法时，都可以使用它。这是自由探索。慢慢弹相邻白键，看符头在线和间之间交替移动，音名字母表就会变得更直观。
zh.sf.editorial.home.connect.p2: 声音能加强联系，却不能代替读谱。识别完记谱位置后，再听琴键的声音，判断音高上行、下行还是不变。保持舒适音量，慢慢练习。虚拟键盘足以完成认音；以后使用实体钢琴，还会加入触键、手指移动和双手协调。
zh.sf.editorial.home.practice.title: 让短时间练习也有明确收获
zh.sf.editorial.home.practice.p0: 每次只设一个小目标，例如认出高音谱表的五条线，或找到当前音域内所有的 C。先花一分钟探索，再做一小组不看提示的练习。把成绩当作下一步学习的线索：熟悉音符上的高分值得高兴，新谱号上的低分也可能意味着你正在学习新东西。
zh.sf.editorial.home.practice.p1: 答错后不要随意乱按，直到碰巧答对。说出正确音名，重新定位，并比较最初答案。是差了一个线间位置、读错谱号，还是高了一个八度？明确错误类型，下一次尝试才有方向，比机械增加答题数量更有效。
zh.sf.editorial.home.practice.p2: 结束前离开测验，读一个小音型，例如 C–D–E–D–C。先念音名，再找琴键，用均匀的拍子弹出来。熟悉字母后，可以进入高音或低音专门练习，扩大音域。读谱指南将继续介绍时值和拍号，让这些独立音高组成真正的乐句。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.title: 让高音谱表变得熟悉
zh.sf.editorial.treble.intro: 先记住可靠的参照点，再读它们之间的位置。稳定的定位方法，比匆忙猜测更有帮助。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.title: 从 G 谱号的参照点开始
zh.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p0: 高音谱号也叫 G 谱号。它的卷曲中心围绕从下往上第二条线，指定这里为 G4。其余线和间按音乐字母表依次排列。每次开始新练习都检查这个参照点。谱号是读谱指令的一部分，不是可以忽略的装饰。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p1: 高音谱表常用于较高音区，包括许多钢琴右手声部，也用于多种乐器和人声。但高音谱号不意味着每个音必须由右手弹。钢琴乐谱可以随音区改变谱号；选择哪只手、什么指法，与识别音高是不同的问题。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.landmarks.p2: 建立三个起点：谱表下方加一线上的中央 C、第二线上的 G4、第三间的 C5。先在键盘上找到它们，再回到谱表。这些参照音把音域分成几个小区域。遇到陌生音时，从最近的已知位置出发，不用每次都从底部数很远。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.lines.title: 按顺序认识线和间
zh.sf.editorial.treble.lines.p0: 高音谱表五条线从下往上是 E4、G4、B4、D5、F5。英语口诀 Every Good Boy Does Fine 可帮助记住 E–G–B–D–F。你也可以自编顺口句，但必须明确从下往上的顺序。口诀只是记忆辅助，并不是旋律必须遵循的运动规则。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.lines.p1: 四个间从下往上是 F4、A4、C5、E5，拼成 FACE。线和间其实交错组成一条连续序列：E4、F4、G4、A4、B4、C5、D5、E5、F5。练习完整序列，不要把线上音和间内音当作两套无关系统。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.lines.p2: 看符头，不要看符干或符尾。中央线上是 B4，无论符干朝上还是朝下。符头若在两条线之间，就属于那个间，即使符干穿过了其他线也不会改变。放慢速度、准确定位符头，通常比紧张时更快地念口诀有效。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.title: 读懂五条线以外的音
zh.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p0: 音太高或太低，超出五线谱时，用加线延伸谱表。中央 C（C4）位于高音谱表下加一线。D4 在这条加线与底线之间的间，E4 在底线上。把 C4–D4–E4 看作相连的三音入口，比单独记三个位置更容易。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p1: 谱表上方，G5 在顶线上面的间，A5 在上加一线。音名字母表继续循环，没有新规则。每移到下一条线或下一个间，前进一个字母。数加线时也要数间；只数短线会跳过一个音，导致答案偏高三度。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.ledger.p2: 八度编号区分相同字母的不同音高。C4 和 C5 都是 C，但对应不同琴键。数字在 B 上行到 C 时改变，因此 B4 后是 C5。练习要求特定音高时，请同时检查字母与编号。音名正确但八度错误，提示你需要强化音区辨认。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.title: 把单个音读成旋律形状
zh.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p0: 能找到单音后，开始观察它们的关系。E4–F4–G4 逐级上行，位置为线、间、线；E4–G4–B4 按三度上行，始终在线上。你往往能先看出形状，再逐个说出音名。准确定位首音，再沿形状读下去，谱表就成了运动地图。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p1: 重复音也很重要。同一位置连续出现的符头保持同一音高，即使节奏不同。旋律还可能跳跃后回到熟悉位置。弹奏前先找重复内容，可以减少新判断的数量，把更多注意力留给节奏和稳定的拍子。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.patterns.p2: 升号、降号、还原号改变音高，却不改变音名字母在谱表上的位置。升 F 仍写在 F 的线或间，由变音记号或调号说明升高。学习变音时，先认字母，再应用记号，避免把黑键误认为一种全新的谱表位置。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.practice.title: 一套专注的高音谱号练习
zh.sf.editorial.treble.practice.p0: 开始时不看提示找到 G4、C5 和中央 C，再围绕一个参照音练习小范围，例如 E4 到 A4。位置稳定后才扩大音域。立即混入所有音高，会让你难以判断问题来自某个陌生音、加线计数，还是一次引入太多内容。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.practice.p1: 认真尝试后再查看答案，把它当作教学步骤。比较正确位置和自己的预期，念出音名后进入下一题。记下容易混淆的音，尤其相邻的线和间。下次先在键盘探索器中比较这些音，再测验。修正错误比维持连对纪录更重要。
zh.sf.editorial.treble.practice.p2: 最后用舒适速度读五个音，保持均匀节拍，不因小犹豫完全停下。可以把 C4–D4–E4–D4–C4 每音弹一拍。熟练后改变节奏或起音，一次只改一个变量。接着探索低音谱号，看看钢琴谱另一半如何连到同一键盘。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.title: 带着明确方向读低音谱号
zh.sf.editorial.bass.intro: 低音谱表使用同一套字母。建立新的参照点，便能独立阅读，并理解整架钢琴的音域。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.title: 低音谱号改变的究竟是什么
zh.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p0: 低音谱号把与高音谱号不同的音高分配给谱表位置。两个圆点夹着从上往下第二条线，指定这里为 F3，因此又叫 F 谱号。开始低音练习时先注意这两个点。套用高音谱号的记忆去读低音谱号，会得出错误音高。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p1: 低音谱表适合较低音乐音域，包括低音人声、大提琴、巴松，以及许多钢琴左手声部。低音不等于简单：它可以承载旋律、建立和声或提供节奏型。独立阅读低音，有助于发现只注意上方旋律时容易遗漏的音乐信息。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.orientation.p2: 钢琴谱表并不永久属于某只手。左手经常演奏低音谱号内容，但谱号描述音高范围，不描述手指。练习时先认出书写音高并找到琴键，再根据乐谱、指法和前后语境决定用哪只手，以及如何舒适地移动。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.title: 用 F3、线与间定位
zh.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p0: 低音谱表五条线从下往上是 G2、B2、D3、F3、A3，可用 Good Boys Do Fine Always 记忆。四个间为 A2、C3、E3、G3，可用 All Cows Eat Grass。念口诀时也念字母，目标是直接认出 G2 或 C3，而不是每次都在脑中背完整句话。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p1: 把 F3 当作中心参照，因为谱号本身指向它。向下一个位置是间内的 E3，向上一个位置是间内的 G3；中央线上是 D3。先练这块紧凑区域，慢弹 D3–E3–F3–G3，看符头在线和间之间交替移动。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.landmarks.p2: 另一个参照是从下往上第二间的 C3。把它与谱表上方的中央 C（C4）比较：字母相同，八度不同。在键盘上同时找到两者，可避免把所有 C 当成一个键。遇到难题时，从附近参照音逐个数线和间。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.register.title: 连接加线与中央 C
zh.sf.editorial.bass.register.p0: 中央 C 在低音谱表上加一线。它下方，B3 在顶线上方的间，A3 在顶线上。A3–B3–C4 是通往高音谱表的实用桥梁。高音谱表下方的中央 C 与低音谱表上方的中央 C 是同一个琴键，不是相邻的两个 C。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.register.p1: 低音谱表下方，F2 在底线下面的间，E2 在下加一线。继续下行时字母逆序为 E、D、C、B、A、G、F。八度编号在 C 下行到 B 时减一，例如 C3 向下是 B2，不是 B3。这是音区标记规则，不是字母表改变。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.register.p2: 许多钢琴乐谱用花括号连接高音与低音谱表，形成大谱表。可以把它们理解为连续音域中的两个阅读窗口。低音上方与高音下方的音域可以重叠，谱号选择也服务于可读性。两行谱表之间的纸面空白会变化，不代表某个固定音乐音程。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.title: 看出低音线条的形状
zh.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p0: 用音程而非孤立字母阅读，低音声部会更清晰。从一条线到下一条线是三度，线到相邻间是级进。试试 C 大三和弦的 C3–E3–G3，它们都在间里；再比较在线上的 D3–F3–A3。音名不同，间距形状却相同。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p1: 伴奏可能在低音根音与和弦之间交替，也可能在根音和五音之间移动。演奏前先找重复音与反复形状，同时仍需读变音记号和节奏。不要假设每个最低音都是当前和弦根音；转位和流动低音可以把其他和弦音放在下面。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.patterns.p2: 多个符头垂直堆叠时，也要纵向阅读。它们通常同时发声形成和弦，而不是快速依次弹奏。先认最低音，再看上方音程。遇到陌生跨度，可以先在键盘探索器分别听每个音，再把它们组合起来，逐步建立同时弹奏的协调能力。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.practice.title: 先练准确，再加手部动作
zh.sf.editorial.bass.practice.p0: 即使高音读得很熟，也应留一部分时间单独练低音谱号。从 F3、D3、C3 开始，再加入邻近音。起初只需念音名并选择琴键。认音时不必同时弹复杂左手音型，把难点分开，才更容易知道错误出在哪里。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.practice.p1: 答错后依次检查谱号、线间位置和八度。总是回答高音谱号音名，就花一分钟回到 F3 参照点；字母正确但音区错误，就比较键盘上两个同名音。让反馈决定下一步练什么，而不只是重新开始计分。
zh.sf.editorial.bass.practice.p2: 结束前完成一个小音乐任务，例如等时值弹 C3–G2–C3–E3，慢慢保持拍子，听每次移动的方向。以后把单个低音与简单高音旋律结合。和弦查找器帮助你听低音如何支撑和声，读谱指南则补充完整乐句需要的节奏知识。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.title: 理解每个钢琴和弦背后的音符
zh.sf.editorial.chords.intro: 选择根音，比较和弦性质，仔细聆听。关键是发现：只改变一个音，为什么就会产生不同的声音。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.formula.title: 用根音和公式构成和弦
zh.sf.editorial.chords.formula.p0: 和弦把同时发声、或依次弹奏但被理解为整体的音组合起来。基本三和弦包含根音、三音、五音。根音决定和弦名称。C 大三和弦中，C 是根音，E 是三音，G 是五音。这些名字描述与 C 的关系，不是键盘上的固定位置。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.formula.p1: 查找器把这种关系显示为琴键：选根音与和弦类型，再查看结果。播放前先读音名，把高亮琴键与标签对应，就能把和弦理解为一组音高，而不是死记手型。保持音程距离，就可以从另一个根音构成相同性质的和弦。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.formula.p2: 音程可以用半音计量，即相邻琴键之间的最小距离，黑白键都要算。C 到升 C 是一个半音，E 到 F 也是一个半音。大三和弦相对根音的位置为 0、4、7 个半音。数移动步数，不把起始键算作第一步，否则每个音程都会少一步。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.quality.title: 听出不同和弦类型改变了什么
zh.sf.editorial.chords.quality.p0: 小三和弦位置为根音上方 0、3、7 个半音。比较 C 大三和弦 C–E–G 与 C 小三和弦 C–降 E–G，只改三音，色彩就变了。大小调是结构名称，不保证音乐一定快乐或悲伤；速度、音区、节奏和周围和声都会影响听感。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.quality.p1: 属七和弦在大三和弦上加小七度，C7 为 C、E、G、降 B。大七和弦则使用本位 B，Cmaj7 为 C、E、G、B。两种符号不能混用。固定根音和音区连续聆听，专注改变的最高音，比比较完全不同的两个和弦更易分辨。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.quality.p2: 挂留和弦替换三音：Csus4 是 C、F、G，Csus2 是 C、D、G。没有 E 或降 E，它们都不是标准大小三和弦。减三和弦和增三和弦还改变五音：C 减为 C、降 E、降 G；C 增为 C、E、升 G。每次只引入一种，指出移动了哪个键。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.title: 保持和弦，改变最低音
zh.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p0: 转位把和弦重新排列，让根音以外的音成为最低音。C–E–G 是原位 C 大三和弦，E–G–C 是第一转位，G–C–E 是第二转位。音名集合仍为 C、E、G。通过转位控制比较这些排列，听不同低音如何改变同一和声的重心。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p1: 斜线符号可以明确指定低音。C/E 表示以 E 为低音的 C 大三和弦，不是先弹 C 和弦再弹 E 和弦。读歌曲和弦谱时，这有助于理解低音移动而和声仍相近的情况。先检查最低高亮琴键，再找上方其余和弦音。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.inversions.p2: 指法数字表示建议手位，不定义和弦。双手都从拇指到小指编号 1 至 5。舒适指法取决于手大小、音区、转位和前后音符。把显示指法作为起点，不要勉强伸展。决定舒适动作前，可以先分别练习各音高。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.title: 把和弦听成一个进行
zh.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p0: 和弦进行是有顺序的和弦序列。C–G–Am–F 依次使用 C 大、G 大、A 小、F 大三和弦，在 C 大调中常标为 I–V–vi–IV。罗马数字描述音级根音与和弦性质，因此换调后仍能识别同一结构。这里大写代表大三和弦，小写 vi 代表小三和弦。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p1: 比较 G–D–Em–C，它在 G 大调中同样是 I–V–vi–IV。音高不同，关系相似。稳定播放两个进行，如果方便，可以哼唱低音根音。关注和弦间的变化，不必给每个声音贴情绪标签；语境本来就是和声趣味的一部分。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.progressions.p2: 转位可以让相邻和弦靠近，减少大跳。例如 C–E–G 可移到 B–D–G，形成以 B 为低音的 G 和弦。最高的 G 保持，另外两音下行，这就是简单的声部进行。先探索邻近位置，不必每次都用原位、大幅跳手。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.practice.title: 练有意义的比较，而不是长清单
zh.sf.editorial.chords.practice.p0: 固定一个根音，比较大三、小三、挂四和弦。聆听前预测哪个音应该改变，再核对高亮并说出全部音名。这样查找器就变成主动练习。只反复播放，声音也许会熟悉，却未必能让你在新和弦谱中看到符号就构成和弦。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.practice.p1: 接着在另一根音上构成相同性质的和弦。黑键名称随语境变化：标准十二平均律中，降 D 与升 C 共用一个键，但和弦拼写仍遵循字母关系。D 大三和弦的三音应写升 F，而非降 G，因为 D 到 F 才具有三度的字母距离。
zh.sf.editorial.chords.practice.p2: 最后选两个或四个和弦，以慢拍先整组弹，再分解弹，保持每个和弦占用的总时长一致。若某次转换困难，就单练该连接再回到完整序列。音符练习强化谱表到琴键的联系，读谱指南补充时值知识，把和弦符号变成有节奏的声部。
